summary: Extends the Sieve vacation extension with a :seconds parameter, which allows auto-replies to the same sender more than once in a single day. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: An out-of-office reply that can say how long to wait before replying again to the same person, even less than a day.

subtitle: Lets a Sieve auto-reply wait seconds, not days, before replying to the same sender again.

tldr.problem: The Sieve Vacation extension limits auto-replies to the same sender to one per number of days, which is too coarse when replies are needed more often.
tldr.mechanism: A new :seconds parameter sets the minimum interval in seconds between auto-replies to a given sender, and is used instead of :days.
tldr.outcome: Sieve scripts can reply every half hour or even to every message, with sites free to set minimum and maximum effective values.

today: RFC 6131 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no replacement or update. It extends the Vacation extension in RFC 5230.

sections.title: Why Days Are Too Coarse
sections.content:
The Sieve email filtering language (RFC 5228) has a Vacation extension (RFC 5230) that generates automatic replies to incoming mail. Its :days parameter limits replies to the same sender to one per number of days.

Some cases need replies more often. This extension adds a :seconds parameter for that finer granularity.
sections.eli5: The old rule only lets you say 'wait this many days'. This adds a way to say 'wait this many seconds' instead.

sections.title: The :seconds Parameter
sections.content:
:seconds gives the minimum time, in seconds, between consecutive auto-replies to a given sender. If given, it is used instead of :days and works in a similar way. Using both in the same vacation action MUST result in a Sieve processing error.

The capability string is vacation-seconds, which implies vacation, so a script can leave vacation out of its require list. The value MUST be greater than or equal to 0 and less than 2**31, and every valid value MUST be accepted without error. If both parameters are omitted, a site-defined interval is used.
sections.eli5: You pick either days or seconds for the waiting time, never both at once. The mail system must accept any sensible number you give it.

sections.title: Site Limits and Zero
sections.content:
Sites MAY define a minimum and a maximum effective value. A requested value below the minimum is raised to the minimum, and one above the maximum is lowered to the maximum. A site maximum MUST be at least 86400 (one day).

:seconds 0 means every message gets a reply and no attempt is made to suppress repeats. The base specification forbids :days 0; the change allows an auto-responder as in RFC 6133. If a site imposes a minimum, not every message will receive a reply.
sections.eli5: The mail system can set its own shortest and longest wait. Zero means answer every single message.

sections.title: Examples and Security
sections.content:
One example replies 'I am in a meeting' with :seconds 1800, so the same sender gets a reply at most every half hour. Another uses :handle "auto-resp" :seconds 0 to acknowledge every message received.

Security considerations of RFC 5230 apply. Implementations SHOULD consider how many auto-replies small values (including 0) could generate, and MAY impose additional limits. RFC 3834 discusses this further.
sections.eli5: Replying very often can flood people with messages, so mail systems may put a cap on it.

data.title: Reply at most every half hour
